new_statements.quote: In Mankon we find that Leroy's super high tone does not originate from a falling tone neither can it be said to have developed from any kind of stress pattern since Mankon does not seem to be a stress accent language. [...] It is obvious that this tone is not related to any stress pattern in Mankon either.
new_statements.citation: Mfonyam, Joseph Ngwa. 1989. Tone in orthography: the case of Bafut and related languages. Thèse de Doctorat d'État, Université de Yaoundé. xvi+686 pp.
new_statements.locator: pp. 393-394 (ch. on Mankon tone, discussion of Leroy's 'super high' tone; quote spans bottom of p. 393 to top of p. 394; second sentence p. 394)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (668 PDF pp.) and rendered PDF pp. 390-391 = printed pp. 393-394. Both sentences are on the page images exactly as quoted: bottom of p. 393 "In" / top of p. 394 "Mankon we find that Leroy's super high tone does not originate from a falling tone neither can it be said to have developed from any kind of stress pattern since Mankon does not seem to be a stress accent language." and mid p. 394 (after the Faraclas 1984 and Schuh 1978 remarks) "In Mankon Leroy's super high tone is not related to intonation nor is it limited to grammatical particles. It is obvious that this tone is not related to any stress pattern in Mankon either." Text-layer lines 14804-14882 of match (scanned noise only…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mankon is a tone language (H/L with downstep, upstep, floating tones); it is judged not to be a stress-accent language, and no word-stress position is stated in any opened source. Loanwords map English primary stress onto H tone (Swiri 1998). If any prominence exists it is, per a family-level survey (Anderson 2001), predictable on the first root syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The statement is hedged ('does not seem to be'). Anderson 2001 (family level) reports predictable root-initial prominence, which is not contradictory if that prominence is non-contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in a discussion of Leroy's (1977) Mankon tone rules (super-high tone); no word forms or placement rule given. Supporting: Swiri 1998 p. 73 calls Mankon a tone language in which English primary-stressed syllables are borrowed as H tone. Family-level counterpoint: Anderson 2001 p. 47 says Eastern Grassfields (incl. Ngemba/Mankon) nouns and verbs carry predictable amplitude prominence on the first root syllable (Ngiemboon examples).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement concerns Mankon proper (Glottolog dialect mank1253, the reference lect of ngem1255) as described by Leroy 1977. Swiri 1998 also describes Mankon; Ngum 1997 describes the Njong dialect (njon1238). Anderson 2001 is a family-level claim for Eastern Grassfields that lists 'Ngemba (Bafut, Mankon,...)' in scope but draws its examples from Ngiemboon (ngie1240), so it is not a Mankon statement. Mfonyam 1989 is a Bafut (bafu1246) thesis whose author also gathered Mankon, Nkwen and Bambili tone data.

sources.citation: Swiri Ade, Roseta. 1998. Lexical expansion in the Mankon language. Mémoire de Maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé I. ix+106 pp. (MPG PuRe item_403505, hdl 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7FA7-2)
sources.note: Sec. 4.2.2 'Harmonisation of prosody' p. 73 (PDF p. 82, verified on page image): 'The Mankon language being an African language is no exception for being a tone language. Loan-words from these stress-timed languages are compelled to bear tones. H tones are marked where syllables bearing primary stress are borrowed. The unstressed syllable bears L or M tones.' Sec. 1.5 Tones pp. 19-20 (H, L, HL, LH); no native stress statement.
